chapters.title: Chapter 5: Building a Forward-Looking Investment Framework

lessons.title: Critical Minerals and Rare Earths: China's Leverage and the Scramble for Alternatives

children.text: In September 2010, after Japan detained a Chinese fishing boat captain near a disputed set of islands, China quietly stopped shipping rare earth elements to Japanese customers for roughly two months. No formal ban was ever announced. Japanese electronics and auto manufacturers, who depended on Chinese rare earths for magnets, batteries and specialty alloys, simply found their orders were not being filled. That episode, more than a decade before the export control toolkit Chapter 2 examined in detail, was the first modern proof that a raw material chokepoint could be turned into diplomatic leverage overnight. It remains the reference case for understanding why critical minerals now sit near the top of every serious supply chain risk assessment.

body.text: Rare earths are not actually rare underground. They are rare in usable form, because separating and refining them is dirty, technically difficult and concentrated almost entirely in one country. That processing chokepoint, not the mining itself, is where the real leverage sits.

children.text: China's Dominance: Mining Is the Smaller Story

markDefs.definition: A group of 17 chemical elements, the lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium, essential for high-strength permanent magnets, batteries and specialty electronics, valuable not because they are geologically scarce but because separating them into pure, usable form is technically difficult and environmentally intensive.

children.text: China mines roughly 60% to 70% of the world's

, down from well over 90% a decade ago as mines in the US and Australia have ramped up. Mining share alone understates China's real leverage badly. The more decisive number is refining and separation: China processes an estimated 85% to 90% of the world's rare earths into usable form, regardless of where the raw ore was originally dug up. A rare earth mine in California or Australia is only half the supply chain. If the separated, purified output still has to be sent to China for processing, the mine has not actually removed the chokepoint.

children.text: China has used this leverage repeatedly since 2010, and the pace has picked up directly in response to the export controls Chapter 2 covered from the other direction. In July 2023, China imposed export licensing requirements on gallium and germanium, materials critical for semiconductors, fibre optics and some defence and solar applications. In December 2023, it added controls on certain graphite products, a material central to EV battery anodes. In 2024, it extended restrictions to antimony, used in flame retardants, ammunition and battery technology. Each move followed a tightening of US chip export controls, making unmistakably clear that critical minerals are China's mirror-image answer to Washington's semiconductor restrictions.

children.text: The response has mirrored the industrial policy playbook from Chapter 2 almost exactly. MP Materials operates Mountain Pass, the only significant rare earth mine currently active in the United States, and has been building domestic separation and magnet manufacturing capacity to close the processing gap this lesson has emphasised. Lynas Rare Earths, based in Australia, runs the largest rare earth mine outside China at Mount Weld and has built a processing plant in Malaysia, alongside a new heavy rare earths separation facility in Texas backed by US Department of Defense funding. These efforts are real, but the timeline is genuinely long: building environmentally permitted mining and, more importantly, processing capacity from a near-standing start typically takes a decade or more, which is why China's leverage is expected to remain significant well into the rest of this decade even as these alternatives scale up.

body.text: India holds the world's fifth largest rare earth reserves, roughly 6% to 7% of the global total, mined mostly as monazite sand along the coasts of Kerala, Odisha and Tamil Nadu through the state-owned monopoly IREL. Despite this reserve base, India's processing capacity has historically lagged its resource endowment badly, and a National Critical Mineral Mission approved in recent years aims to close that gap. Given how quickly this specific initiative is evolving, verify its current funding and project status against recent government sources rather than treating this as settled.

body.title: Identify the real chokepoint
body.question: Country A mines a large share of the world's raw rare earth ore but has to ship nearly all of it to Country B for separation and refining before it becomes usable. Which country holds the greater strategic leverage over the global supply chain?
options: Country A, because it controls the raw material at the source
Country B, because refining and separation is the harder-to-replicate, more concentrated step
Neither, since mining and refining carry equal leverage
It depends only on which country has lower labour costs
body.explanation: This lesson's central point is that processing, not mining, is where rare earth leverage actually concentrates. A mine without domestic refining capacity, like several Western rare earth projects historically, still leaves the country dependent on the refiner, exactly the dynamic that has made China's roughly 85% to 90% share of global processing so strategically significant.

body.title: Size the processing gap
body.prompt: China accounts for roughly 60% of global rare earth mining but roughly 87% of global rare earth processing and separation capacity. What is the difference, in percentage points, between its processing share and its mining share?
body.explanation: 87 minus 60 is approximately 27 percentage points. That gap is the single clearest numerical illustration of this lesson's core argument, China's dominance in the finished, usable material is significantly larger than its dominance in the raw ore, which is exactly why new mines outside China alone do not solve the strategic dependency.

cards.definition: A group of 17 elements essential for high-strength magnets, batteries and electronics, valuable because separating them into usable form is difficult and heavily concentrated in China, not because they are geologically scarce.
A concentration of refining or separation capacity, as opposed to raw material extraction, that gives a country strategic leverage even when mining itself is more geographically diversified.

Using export control over a raw material as diplomatic or economic leverage, first demonstrated at scale in China's 2010 rare earth response to Japan and repeated with gallium, germanium, graphite and antimony since 2023.

points: China's real leverage over rare earths comes from processing dominance, roughly 85% to 90% of global separation capacity, far more than its roughly 60% to 70% share of raw mining.
China's 2010 unofficial rare earth embargo on Japan is the foundational case study for critical mineral leverage, predating the export control toolkit examined in Chapter 2 by over a decade.
Since 2023, China has extended export restrictions to gallium, germanium, graphite and antimony, moves widely read as a direct mirror response to Western semiconductor export controls.
Alternative supply chains led by MP Materials in the US and Lynas Rare Earths in Australia and Malaysia are real but face decade-long timelines to build genuine processing capacity, not just mining.
India holds the world's fifth largest rare earth reserves but has historically underdeveloped processing capacity relative to that resource base, a gap recent government initiatives aim to close.

When assessing any critical mineral supply chain story, always ask separately about mining share and processing share, since this lesson's data shows they can tell very different stories about where the real dependency sits.
